instructions:
You turn a task's text into atomic, machine-checkable requirements. For each item you
get the task text, the task kind, the reference solution (it satisfies the task), the
initial workspace, and what the reference produced (files, stdout, exit status, tool
calls, final state). You are not shown how the task is graded and must not guess.

Write one requirement per distinct obligation in the task text (outputs, their
content, required steps, ordering constraints, prohibited actions, policies). Each
requirement has an "id" (R1, R2, ...), "text" (the obligation in plain words, quoting
the task where possible), and "checks": a list of typed checks that pass on the
reference outcome and fail when the obligation is broken. Allowed check types and
fields: file_exists {path}; file_absent {path}; file_equals {path, text, normalize:
none|strip|trailing_ws}; file_contains {path, text}; file_regex {path, pattern};
file_json {path, pointer, equals, lenient}; file_lines {path, count};
stdout_contains {text}; stdout_regex {pattern}; stdout_json {pointer, equals,
lenient}; exit_code {code}; call {probe: {function, args, kwargs}, equals} or
{probe, matches_reference: true}; same_as_reference {target: stdout|state|file:<path>,
normalize}; trajectory_includes {tool, args}; trajectory_excludes {tool, args};
trajectory_before {first: {tool, args}, then: {tool, args}}; state_equals {pointer,
equals}.

Be exactly as strict as the task text. If the text demands an exact format, check it
exactly; if it only asks for content, check content (use "normalize" or "lenient" so
that harmless formatting does not fail the check). For function tasks, add call
probes on the examples in the text and on a few further valid inputs, using
matches_reference for inputs whose expected output the text does not state. Return
for each item: {"requirements": [ ... ]}.

Use `update_shipping_address` to set the shipping address of order `ORD-55120` to exactly this one-line string:

# Transpose a TSV table

`matrix.tsv` is a tab-separated table in which every row has the same number of cells. Write `transposed.tsv` with rows and columns swapped: the cell in row i, column j of the output is the cell in row j, column i of the input.

Write the output in the same format: cells separated by a single tab character, every row (including the last) terminated by a newline, and cell text unchanged (cells may contain spaces).

# Open a helpdesk ticket

You are working the IT helpdesk queue. Ana Lima (ana.lima@example.com) writes:

> Since this morning the office VPN drops every few minutes and I have to log in again each time.

Use the helpdesk tools to:

1. Look up Ana's user record with `find_user`.
2. Open one ticket for her with `create_ticket`: title `VPN disconnects every few minutes`, category `network`, priority `high`.
3. Assign the new ticket to the `netops` team with `assign_ticket`.

Tickets are numbered in sequence; the next ticket created will be `T-1001`. Do not modify any existing ticket.

Tools (see `support/env.py`):

- `find_user(email)`
- `create_ticket(user_id, title, category, priority)`
- `assign_ticket(ticket_id, team)`
- `add_comment(ticket_id, text)`
- `get_ticket(ticket_id)`

# Normalize dates from supplier invoices

Supplier invoices write dates in different ways. Write a Python module `dateparse.py` with a function `to_iso_date(text)` that returns the date as an ISO string `YYYY-MM-DD`.

Accepted input formats (surrounding spaces are ignored):

- `Month D, YYYY`, where Month is an English month name, either in full (`March`) or as its three-letter abbreviation (`Mar`), in any capitalization, and D has one or two digits: `"March 5, 2026"` gives `"2026-03-05"`.
- `DD/MM/YYYY` (day first, two digits each): `"05/03/2026"` gives `"2026-03-05"`.
- `YYYY.MM.DD`: `"2026.03.05"` gives `"2026-03-05"`.

Raise `ValueError` for anything else, including dates that do not exist such as `"31/04/2026"`.

reference_solution.solve.py:
import json

config = {}
with open("app.env", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    for raw in fh.read().split("\n"):
        line = raw.strip(" \t")
        if not line or line.startswith("#"):
            continue
        key, _, value = line.partition("=")
        key, value = key.strip(" \t"), value.strip(" \t")
        if len(value) >= 2 and value[0] == value[-1] and value[0] in "\"'":
            value = value[1:-1]
        config[key] = value

with open("config.json", "w", encoding="utf-8") as fh:
    json.dump(config, fh, indent=2)
    fh.write("\n")

# Convert an env file to JSON

The deployment tool wants its settings as JSON. Convert `app.env` into `config.json`.

Rules for reading `app.env`:

- Ignore blank lines and lines whose first non-space character is `#`.
- Every other line has the form `KEY=VALUE`, split at the first `=`. Remove spaces and tabs around the key and around the value.
- If the value (after that) starts and ends with the same quote character, `"` or `'`, remove that pair of quotes. Nothing else is unescaped.
- If a key appears more than once, the last occurrence wins.

`config.json` must contain a JSON object mapping each key to its value as a string. Formatting and key order are up to you.

# Book the cheapest matching room

Elif Demir wants a room from `2026-12-18` (check-in) to `2026-12-20` (check-out).

Book the cheapest room that is available for those dates, is non-smoking, and has a king bed. Book it under the guest name `Elif Demir` and attach her loyalty number `LY-55821`. Make no other bookings or changes.

Tools (see `support/env.py`):

- `search_rooms(check_in, check_out)`: rooms available for the whole stay, with bed type, smoking flag, and nightly price
- `create_booking(room, guest_name, check_in, check_out, loyalty_number)`
- `cancel_booking(booking_id)`
